title: Pakistan Summons Imran Khan's Sister After Remarks on Army's Inability to Defeat India
excerpt: Aleema Khan faces fresh legal action over controversial statements questioning Pakistan's military performance during the 2025 conflict with India and her praise of Prime Minister Modi's leadership.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Aleema Khan has been summoned for questioning the Pakistan Army's capabilities against India during the 2025 conflict.
  • Her remarks included praise for PM Modi, drawing backlash from Pakistan's military establishment.
  • Imran Khan, her brother, has been imprisoned since August 2023, facing over 30 years in sentences.
  • Aleema is charged with creating divisions between the people and the army under Pakistan's legal code.
  • Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency has summoned Aleema Khan, sister of jailed former PM Imran Khan, on charges of "anti-state speech" for remarks questioning the Pakistan Army's capabilities against India.
  • Aleema reportedly claimed the Pakistan military could not defeat India during the 2025 conflict and expressed support for PM Modi's governance, drawing sharp backlash from the establishment.
  • The summons marks the latest in a series of legal actions against the Khan family, with Imran Khan imprisoned since August 2023 and facing over 30 years in combined sentences.
  • Aleema has been charged with "creating divisions between the people and the army" under Pakistan's Code of Criminal Procedure.

Fresh Summons for Anti-Army Remarks

Pakistan's authorities have summoned Aleema Khan, the outspoken sister of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan, after she made controversial remarks questioning the Pakistan Army's military capabilities against India during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict and expressed admiration for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership.

The Federal Investigation Agency initiated an inquiry against Aleema for allegedly "creating a divide" between the people and the Pakistani armed forces, according to The Express Tribune. The notice, issued under Section 160 of Pakistan's Code of Criminal Procedure, charged her with "creating divisions between the people and the army by criminal conspiracy and anti-state speech."

The summons was issued at the request of Pakistan's Ministry of Interior and directed Aleema to appear at the FIA Headquarters in Islamabad. Aleema received the notice at her Lahore residence, though she has a history of skipping such summons — she previously failed to appear before the FIA Cyber Crime Wing when summoned for allegedly spreading "fear and panic" in society.

What Aleema Khan Said

Aleema Khan has been increasingly vocal in her criticism of Pakistan's military establishment, particularly Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. In public statements and on social media, she questioned the Pakistan Army's performance during the brief but intense conflict with India in May 2025.

Her remarks took direct aim at the military's official narrative that Pakistan successfully countered India's Operation Sindoor. She suggested the military leadership under Munir had led the country into a conflict it could not win, and praised Modi's governance model — statements that cross red lines in Pakistan's civil-military discourse.

"Whenever Imran Khan comes to power, you will see that he always tries to befriend India and even the BJP. Whenever there is this radical Islamist, Asim Munir, you will see that there will be war with India."

— Aleema Khan, in an interview on Sky News

In her Sky News appearance, Aleema described her brother as a "pure liberal" and an "asset to the West," contrasting him with Munir, whom she called a "radicalised Islamist" whose "conservatism forces him to fight against those who don't believe in Islam," according to Hindustan Times.

The 2025 India-Pakistan Conflict

The remarks directly challenge Pakistan's military narrative around the May 2025 conflict — the worst confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in decades.

The conflict was triggered by an attack on tourists in Pahalgam, Indian-administered Kashmir, in April 2025, which India blamed on Pakistan. New Delhi launched air strikes in early May, followed by a four-day exchange of missiles, drones, and artillery fire before a US-brokered ceasefire halted hostilities, according to Reuters.

Pakistan branded its response "Operation Bunyanum Marsoos" and claimed India failed to achieve its objectives. India said Operation Sindoor degraded terrorist infrastructure and accused Pakistan of launching a post-conflict disinformation campaign through ISI-linked social media handles.

A Family Under Siege

The summons adds to mounting legal troubles for the Khan family. Imran Khan has been imprisoned at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi since August 2023 and faces combined sentences exceeding 30 years — including 14 years in a £190 million corruption case and 17 years in the Toshakhana-2 case. His family alleges he has been held in solitary confinement and denied access to visitors, books, and television.

Aleema faces non-bailable arrest warrants from an anti-terrorism court over the November 2024 protest case, where she was named prime accused for allegedly inciting PTI supporters to demonstrate despite a Section 144 ban. The Islamabad High Court had earlier restrained the FIA from "harassing" Aleema, but the latest summons suggests the establishment is escalating pressure as PTI agitates for its founder's release.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, an admission from within the family of a former Pakistani prime minister that Pakistan's military could not match India's capabilities — combined with praise for Modi — underscores shifting power dynamics in South Asia following the 2025 conflict.

The episode highlights deepening fissures in Pakistan's political system, where dissent against the military is increasingly criminalised. The Khan family's battles have drawn attention from Amnesty International, which condemned the detention of PTI supporters and described restrictions on Imran Khan's access as "unlawful and inhumane." As Pakistan grapples with economic instability and diplomatic isolation, the crackdown raises questions about whether Islamabad is suppressing inconvenient truths about its strategic vulnerabilities.
